evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.7.1: ex litterīs tuīs … cēpī ūnā cum omnibus incrēdibilem voluptātem
Cic. Fin. 1.37 (Lewis & Short): omne id, quō gaudēmus, voluptās est
Cic. Fam. 14.1.4: utinam ea rēs eī voluptātī sit!
terms.comment: Pleasure of every kind, of the body or of the mind; the philosophers’ word for ἡδονή, so in moral writing often the pleasure one should not chase. “It gives me pleasure”: voluptātem capiō ex, or mihi voluptātī est. In comedy voluptās mea is “my darling” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.105 (Lewis & Short): homō videndī et audiendī dēlectātiōne dūcitur
terms.comment: The delight a thing gives, especially of seeing, hearing and learning; it never has the bad sense voluptās can have. The verb is dēlectāre (see enjoy).

phrases.latin: ex litterīs tuīs, quās pūblicē mīsistī, cēpī ūnā cum omnibus incrēdibilem voluptātem
phrases.english: your official letter gave me, as it gave everyone, enormous pleasure

phrases.latin: cibī pōtiōnisque dēsīderiō nātūrālī, nōn voluptāte modus fīnītus
phrases.english: the measure of his food and drink was set by natural need, not by pleasure
